answer: On arrival, index each prototype’s spare output, missing input, and setup time. Match compatible handoffs across unlike subjects. Another design pairs two failures that disappear under the same constraint. Monday, open one cross-subject pair and one same-subject pair, four originals total. A bicycle counter emits one click per wheel turn. A stalled audio tour needs a distance trigger. Tape the counter to a cart and advance the tour every hundred clicks. Spend five minutes per pair sketching its first observable demonstration. Favor the pair whose handoff can be faked immediately and whose remaining parts fit the afternoon.

The visitor could carry a rhythm learned at one half into a challenge at the other. Or let two independently usable shadow experiments overlap. First volunteer mails a postcard with a full-scale sample of a transparent striped slider and its viewing-window dimensions. Second returns a transparent sample with slightly closer stripes, marked with a common alignment edge. Alone, either slider reveals how bar shadows shift. Dock them together and a millimeter of travel sends broad dark bands racing across the window. Before installation each volunteer can try both postcard patterns against a window. Compare band travel with one pattern removed at the same slider speed.

Try sound-first auditions behind a screen, or give everyone a tiny musical job with several possible tools. Use the jobs. First, write down your expected choice. Draw a role such as ‘sound like footsteps receding.’ Each station has a picture of the grip, a three-sound challenge, and a packing diagram. In pairs, spend twenty minutes trying three unfamiliar candidates. Swap player and listener. The listener faces away and points when the footsteps vanish. Spend the final twenty minutes independently unpacking, playing, and repacking a favorite before choosing whether to borrow. Give alternating pairs ordinary free browsing. Count unexpected checkouts whose borrowers complete the solo repeat.

One approach grows a family tree by reversing an assumption at each fork. Another schedules six different experiences of the same idea, such as repairing it, refusing it, or inheriting it. Use the tree. Save each discarded passage verbatim under a short designer-chosen name. On return, show one ancestor and optionally one recalled discard. List fork names only. Mark assumptions already reversed. For a communal lamp, reversing ownership yields a lamp that circulates. Reversing who signals whom yields a lamp that asks for company. Choosing ‘circulates’ restores its exact text. Across returns compare against ordinary continuation by counting directions that demand a different prototype.

Either index failed prototypes by what would rescue them, or stage a swap meet of spare parts. Use the rescue index. On arrival extract one missing input, one incidental output and an afternoon-sized test from each note. Match stored cards where an output supplies a missing input across unrelated projects. Monday, show two pairs with their proposed handoffs. Open exactly those four originals to check units and effort. A stalled queue display needs an arrival pulse. An abandoned door chime already counts entries. Replay chime counts into the display before lunch. Compare against two title-similar pairs on another Monday, counting working handoffs by closing time.

One scheme swaps scores for a visitor to perform across both halves. Another uses visitors’ shadows as a shared signal. Agree on one patch of floor. Each postcard diagrams where its half casts light or senses shadow there, including solo behavior. One half sweeps a light across the patch to demonstrate rotation. The other counts interruptions on a dial and works alone with a steady lamp and a waving hand. Together the dial measures rotation until a visitor’s fingers make one sweep register as several moons. Rehearse with a flashlight, cardboard and tally marks. Compare whether visitors predict counts with the halves coupled versus displayed side by side.

Try an anonymous sound ballot, or let pairs trade musical jobs halfway through a duet. Use the trade. In five minutes everyone names their expected choice. Place instruments in pairs with picture cards for two easy parts, a pulse and an answer. Partners try each job, swap instruments, then rotate twice over thirty minutes. Someone drawn to melody discovers they like answering a pulse with a single drum roll. Spend fifteen minutes letting each person choose and teach their partner how to start alone. Reserve ten minutes for checkout, including the duet card. Compare with free browsing on unexpected loans whose borrowers can independently restart their part.

One design starts each visit with a fresh sketch before revealing any history. Another keeps a six-slot map of design decisions. Use the map. Each exit saves the exact passage under a designer-chosen handle and marks one decision the passage assumed. On return, pick an unused reversal from short labels, then read the passage it challenges. If “bus stop” assumed everyone waits together, try a stop that travels between waiting people. A handle retrieves its original verbatim, using the second reading slot. Compare six returns against showing the two latest passages. Have the designer group unlabeled sketches by mechanism and time a discarded-sketch lookup.

One option draws two pairs from unrelated shelves. Another indexes what each prototype produced and the exact missing input that stopped it. On addition, record those two fields, domain, dependencies and a five-minute check. New entries can retire a dependency by identifier. Monday, deal two cross-domain producer–consumer pairs with matching formats and no known retired dependency; open those four originals. A stalled bird-call quiz needs timestamped clips; a meeting recorder exports them. Spend five minutes feeding one clip through, then five choosing the pair with a visible afternoon demo. Across Mondays, alternate this deal with random cross-shelf pairs and count working demos by dinner.

Either build call-and-response drums that trade rhythms, or build two windows whose moving shadows race farther than either window moves. Choose the windows. Each postcard carries a transparent working miniature, an alignment cross and the stripe spacing. One volunteer builds a 2 mm striped slider, the other a 2.2 mm screen, both sized to the same opening. Alone, visitors trace a stripe. Together, sliding one stripe width sends a broad dark band across several fingers. A late builder’s postcard can stand in at the tabletop. Before fabrication, overlap the postcards, then compare with one alone. Can visitors make a band outrun their hand?

Try a curtain concert where beginners choose by sound, or give everyone an instrument they initially passed over and a partner who needs its sound. Spend ten minutes browsing and marking first choices. Partners then draw an unchosen instrument apiece from the available pile. Allow fifteen minutes with illustrated setup cards to make a two-sound doorbell together. For twenty minutes, swap roles, then each packs, unpacks and plays their own part unaided. The facilitator troubleshoots. Reserve fifteen minutes for voluntary checkout with cards. Alternate tables between drawing and free choice. Count borrowers who independently restart a previously unchosen instrument and take it home.

Offer a branching map of discarded proposals, or deal a six-visit deck of design questions. Use the deck. On visit one, pick six distinct angles together. On each return, reveal an unused angle and two verbatim passages: one constraint the designer kept, one earlier decision this angle could overturn. For a lamp, pair “must fit a pocket” with “the owner controls it”; ask who else might control the light. Every discard gets a short receipt linked to its immutable passage. Redeeming it replaces one reading slot. Compare with two most-recent passages across six visits; have a blind reviewer group proposals by mechanism and check a redeemed receipt character-for-character.

Run a parts exchange, or draw two failures with the same symptom and ask whether one fix rescues both. For the exchange, read each prototype once. File what it produces, what it lacks, its field, and one five-minute compatibility check. New entries can supersede old claims by ID. Match offers to needs across fields. A shutter tester emits timed light pulses. A stalled tabletop railway needs a crossing signal. Can its detector count ten flashes? Monday, open that pair and the closest same-topic pair. Give each five minutes. Choose whichever demonstrates a handoff and leaves an afternoon-sized build.

Make two transparent stripe wheels that produce a third moving pattern when overlaid, or build a relay where one visitor’s recorded rhythm becomes the next visitor’s prediction game. For the wheels, give both volunteers the same postcard-sized mounting template with a center pinhole and circular track. One builds 24 radial stripes and the other 25. Each mails a tracing of their wheel and keeps the original. Alone, spin either wheel against the received tracing. Together, visitors turn separate handles and chase the dark band that appears between the patterns. Alternate overlay and side-by-side trials. Can visitors reverse the band’s travel while both handles still turn clockwise?

Offer a sound-matching game behind a screen, or issue everyone a ticket to an instrument they crossed off on arrival. Use tickets. Spend five minutes marking preferences, fifteen rotating pairs through ticketed stations, twenty rehearsing and twenty teaching back and borrowing. Each station has a picture card for setup, one playable phrase and packing. At a thumb piano, one partner plays three plucks, packs it, then watches the other unpack and answer. The facilitator circulates. Half the pairs start at free-choice stations on the same timetable. At checkout count crossed-off instruments borrowed by people who can independently unpack and play them.

Give the designer six envelopes labeled by different design decisions, or let each return begin with a wager against the last prototype. Use the envelopes. At each exit, bookmark the exact passages for the working constraint and the discarded fork, including versions. Next visit, open an unused envelope and show the constraint plus one relevant fork. With a silent doorbell, an envelope marked “Who notices first?” might yield a light on the visitor’s side so they know someone answered. Naming a discarded fork retrieves its verbatim passage in one slot. Compare six envelope visits with chronological replay. Blind-count distinct mechanisms and check a requested restoration word for word.

Either surface pairs with a rare shared component and dissimilar descriptions, or run a parts exchange. At intake, record what worked, what was missing, signal format, and domain. Match each new card against indexed offers and requests. Monday, open one cross-domain match and one rare-component pair, four originals total. A failed bicycle counter still emits milliseconds between wheel pulses. A stalled percussion toy accepts millisecond intervals. Feed one recorded ride into the toy and see whether someone can tap the uphill stretch. Give each pair five minutes. Score whether the maintainer can specify an available input, compatible connection, and observable afternoon demo before the timer rings.

Exchange overlays that visitors superimpose, or let visitors carry messages between two ecosystems. For the latter, agree on one turn per visitor and two postcards, each naming its outgoing count, units, and sample sequence. The hare station reports animals after births. The lynx station uses yesterday’s hare count to set today’s hunting pressure and returns a kill count. Cap kills at living hares. Either station can open alone using the other’s sample sequence. Together visitors can watch hunting peak after abundance and keep climbing as hares decline. Rehearse with beans and paper. Remove half the hares halfway through and compare the response with simply replaying both postcards.

Try a sound hunt, or have pairs secretly cast each other for a two-instrument duet. For the hunt, everyone first names the instrument they expect to borrow. Spend ten minutes hearing the facilitator play tiny phrases behind a screen. Vote by phrase number before the reveal. Spend twenty minutes trying favorites in pairs, swapping when neither partner discovers a new sound. Use the next twenty to teach a partner a phrase on an unexpected favorite. In the last ten, pack it with its three-picture setup card. Give alternate pairs a labeled menu for the same phrases. Count unexpected loans whose borrowers can unpack and play unaided.

One option rotates constraints drawn from a hat. Another keeps a six-visit ledger of mechanisms actually explored. On return, offer two verbatim excerpts from branches least represented in that ledger. Label each candidate with what it inherits. For a quiet doorbell, keep the silence requirement, reopen a discarded moving-shadow sketch, and try signaling by changing the shape of afternoon light. Each fork inherits only the brief and explicitly selected lines. Give every discarded version a permanent handle. Redeeming it uses one reading slot and restores the stored text exactly. Compare against showing the latest two excerpts. Blind-sort the resulting sketches by mechanism and count distinct piles.

One approach indexes rare shared parts and deals four notes from distant uses of the same part. Another indexes what each prototype produces, what it lacks, and what already works. On insertion, match those fields against saved entries; keep pairs with compatible quantities, different purposes, and one bench test under three hours. A rain gauge’s spare contact closure could advance an abandoned story box one line per drop. Monday, deal four notes as two unlabeled pairs: one functional match and one shared-part match. Allow five minutes per pair to name the connection, locate the parts, and specify an observable result. Build whichever clears all three.

One design trades rhythms: each half answers a visitor’s taps with a changed rhythm that its neighbor can hear. Another lets visitors turn two transparent wheels on separate stands and look through both. Agree on a hub height and postcard-sized window. One volunteer draws 30 evenly spaced spokes, the other 31. Each mails a transparent working postcard with alignment marks. Clip the absent partner’s card behind the first wheel until its stand arrives. Together, a tiny turn sends a dark band racing around the rim. Try equal-spoke and mismatched paper wheels with three visitors; ask each to make the band lap their finger without turning either wheel a full revolution.

One option pairs strangers to find two instruments whose sounds answer each other. Another starts with everyone secretly circling three instruments they’d pass over. Give each instrument a folding card: outside, a sound to chase; inside, a grip sketch and two moves. Spend ten minutes choosing sounds, twenty sampling in pairs, twenty teaching one favorite to a partner, ten checking out. “Footsteps becoming rain” might lead to a cabasa. The borrower demonstrates a slow scrape, a shower, and how to pack it; the card goes home. Give alternate pairs ordinary name cards with identical insides. Count borrowers who choose a circled instrument and repeat both moves unaided.

One design draws a fresh constraint each visit and seals each abandoned draft in a numbered envelope. Another keeps a ledger of mechanisms actually tried. On return, show the original brief and one passage from the least-explored relevant mechanism. The new branch inherits only those two; its label names both. After three clock-controlled lamps, a shelved balance sketch supplies a fourth lamp whose shade tilts toward a book. Discarding freezes its exact text and decisions under a short name. Entering that name spends one passage slot and restores the saved version verbatim. Compare six visits against latest-two recall: blind-sort outputs by operating principle and check one surprise restoration word-for-word.

At intake, record what each prototype consumes, produces, and needs to run. Join compatible ports across different purposes; update connection counts by port. Alternatively, pick maximally different descriptions by extra compressed bytes and let the maintainer invent a link. Prefer the port join. A drawer sensor emits open/close times; a moth-light simulator consumes intervals between events. Replay yesterday’s kitchen rhythm as dusk. On Monday show the connecting sentence and required adapter for two disjoint pairs with uncommon ports and available parts. Open four originals; spend five minutes per pair sketching the hookup. Compare against two random port-compatible pairs on separate Mondays: count working, unanticipated afternoon demos.

Either pass pulses directly or let visitors shuttle colored counters between two rule boards, each responding to accumulated counters. For pulses, each postcard specifies one light flash per local beat, a gentle phase advance on receiving a flash, and a drawn timing example. One builds a flashing firefly, the other a clicking cricket with a beacon. Each oscillates alone; visitors tune their speeds until the forest suddenly beats together. Shield each detector from its own beacon. At installation, uncover the detectors, then cover them again without touching the dials. Count coincident beats in each minute against the simpler explanation of two clocks accidentally matching.

Offer a mystery sound trail or a partner exchange where each beginner teaches their first sound on an unfamiliar instrument. For the trail, spend five minutes writing down first choices. Shuffle starting stations among twenty instruments. Front cards promise effects (“make rain with one hand”); reverse cards show one movement. Explore for twenty minutes, moving after two tries yield nothing new. Spend twenty rebuilding a favorite effect, then fifteen packing and teaching a partner how to start again using the take-home card. The facilitator circulates for sticking points. Alternate mystery and name-first cards at matched stations, swapping halfway; tally unexpected loans whose borrowers independently repeat the effect.

Give each return two old passages: the brief and a passage from the least explored mechanism. Let the designer mark which mechanisms the resulting sketch actually used. Alternatively, let them rewind one decision per visit and take its opposite. Use the first design: after three folding-lamp sketches, surface the shelved counterweight idea. A detour inherits only the displayed pair; save its exact text and sketch under a numbered tab. Reopening that tab spends a passage slot and displays the saved version. Run six visits against a latest-two baseline. Blind-count distinct working mechanisms and ask the designer to recover one discarded sketch verbatim.

Index what each prototype produces and consumes, or pair a randomly drawn failure with the most differently worded workaround. For the index, read each new entry once. Store its domain, tangible inputs and outputs, and cheapest working demo. Join against stored cards on matching output/input; rank rare matches across domains first. Monday open two disjoint pairs. A bicycle counter emits timestamped clicks; a stalled poetry printer needs a rhythm. Feed yesterday’s clicks into the printer and listen to a commute as verse. Hide the rankings and shuffle one matched pair with one keyword-nearest pair. In ten minutes, try to specify a runnable afternoon acceptance test for each.

Overlay independently drawn transparencies, or couple two one-bit machines. For the machines each postcard specifies its builder’s color rule, a worked example and the shared clock: reveal both new colors together. One copies its neighbor’s last color, the other shows the opposite. Alone, a visitor supplies the missing neighbor with a reversible card. Together, start both white. Visitors turn cards face down before revealing: white/black, black/black, black/white, white/white. A machine that only copies has helped make a clock. Try paper cards before construction. Ask visitors to predict four beats, then disconnect one neighbor and hold its input white. Compare with two independent flipping cards.

Try a sound treasure hunt, or let beginners audition for the same musical job on unfamiliar instruments. For the audition, privately circle your first choice. In ten minutes, pairs draw a job (“make footsteps for a giant”) and two instruments neither circled. Each gets a picture showing one safe move. Trade when you can repeat a sound twice or want help. Spend twenty minutes swapping jobs, twenty teaching a partner your favorite sound from scratch, ten packing with its picture. Alternate tables get free browsing and identical pictures. Count borrowers who choose outside their original pick and can restart the sound unaided after packing and unpacking.

Offer a rotating constraint lottery or let neglected questions earn the next turn. For the latter, tally directions actually tried over six visits. On return, show one saved constraint and one passage for the least-tried question. Each fork inherits only those two, shown by title. If earlier umbrella sketches all shed rain, the neglected question “who needs the water?” might yield a handle that waters a planter. Archive each discarded fork verbatim with choices and a numbered tab; tapping it spends a passage slot and restores its saved state. Compare against showing the latest two passages: count distinct mechanisms blindly and verify a restored fork word for word.
